name: Halakha
scope: Halakha as the defining sources present it: the Jewish religious-legal system, covering ritual, civil, criminal and family law, that rabbinic Judaism derives from the Written and Oral Torah (s1, s2). It is represented by the rabbinic tradition's own legal literature, Mishnah, Talmud and the medieval codes (Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, Jacob ben Asher's Tur, Joseph Karo's Shulchan Aruch with Isserles' Mappa), and by the traditional view that the law is binding and traces to Sinai (s1, s2, s3, s4). Where the sources distinguish the movements, the profile follows the halakhic (Orthodox) view, in which the law is binding; Conservative adaptation is a variant and Reform disregard of halakha (s1, s4) is outside it. It does not extend to biblical law alone, to aggadah (the non-legal rabbinic material, s1, s2), to Karaite Judaism, or to Christian or antiquarian books on 'Hebrew law' (e.g. Mackintosh, Crosse) that are not the halakhic tradition's own account.

summary: Halakha is Jewish religious law, the body of commandments derived from the written and oral Torah and developed in the Mishnah, Talmud and later codes such as Maimonides' Mishneh Torah and the Shulhan Arukh. It governs worship, family, civil and criminal matters, diet and ethics. This audit records only positions the codes state, and leaves most statements unanswered.
